runs.text: The Distance That Stayed
“Why don't you ever come and sit with me?”
Anya looked at her father but could not think of an answer. There were many things she could
have said, yet none seemed right. She could have told him that she did not know what to talk
about, that sitting beside him made her uncomfortable, or that she had grown so accustomed to
keeping her distance that being close to him now felt unfamiliar. Instead, she remained silent.
Perhaps he only wanted her company. Perhaps she should have tried harder. But how was she
supposed to begin a conversation with someone she had spent most of her life learning not to
disturb?
Anya could not remember when she had first become afraid of her father. The fear seemed to
have existed for as long as her memories did. He was not always angry, but he was rarely careful
with his words. She had been a sickly child, and her parents often reminded her that simply being
alive was enough. Perhaps they meant to reassure her, but Anya had always dreamed of
achieving something meaningful. She wanted to become someone, to accomplish things she
could be proud of, and perhaps, more than she admitted, to see a little pride in their faces. When
she was younger, she approached her father with the ordinary excitement of a child who wanted
to share everything. But he was often tired and told her to go away. When she came first in her
class, he simply said, “Good.” She had hoped for a smile or another question, but the
conversation ended there. When she wanted a family photograph, he refused. When she asked
for chocolates, the answer was no. She noticed, too, that things seemed different with her three
sisters. None of these moments seemed particularly significant on their own, yet together they
taught her something she had never consciously decided to learn: it was easier not to ask.
Yet Anya could never say that her father did not care for her. When she was sick, he looked after
her, worried about her health, and made sure she had what she needed. Even now, she knew his
concern had not disappeared. Perhaps that was how he understood love, through responsibility
rather than words of affection. She remembered those moments with gratitude, but she had
wanted him to know the other parts of her too. The girl who dreamed beyond her childhood
illnesses, who worked hard for what she believed in, and who sometimes wanted nothing more
than to share a small happiness with her father. As she grew older, she continued telling her
parents about her achievements, hoping their response might change. Their silence, however, left
her regretting the excitement she had shared. Eventually, she stopped telling them about the little
moments of her life. Her room became the place where she felt most comfortable, while
speaking to her father required an effort she could never fully explain.
A few days earlier, Anya had received an award for her research paper. She told her parents,
carrying a little of the excitement she used to feel as a child. They remained silent. There was no
criticism, nothing she could reasonably point to as unkind, yet she regretted telling them almost
immediately. When she later secured an internship as a research assistant, she kept the news to
herself. It seemed easier to enjoy the achievement alone than to wait for a response that might
never come. Eventually, her father found out. “I didn't know that,” he said. Of course he had not
known. She had deliberately kept the news from him. Yet something about his words troubled
her. She had once wanted him to know everything. Had he noticed when she stopped, or had her
silence become so familiar that neither of them questioned it anymore?
Later, when Anya was alone, the familiar argument began. Perhaps he genuinely wanted to know
about her life. But why was it so difficult to tell him? He had cared for her when she was sick,
and she had never forgotten that. Was she being unfair by remembering the things he had not
done more clearly than the things he had? Perhaps she was. But did appreciating his care mean
she should stop wishing for something else? He had been there when she needed him physically.
Why did she still feel so uncertain about approaching him emotionally? Perhaps she expected too
much. Yet what was so unreasonable about wanting her parents to share a little happiness in
something she had worked hard to achieve? She had spent years moving between these thoughts,
never entirely trusting either side. One reminded her of her father's care; the other remembered
the little girl who had wanted his attention and gradually stopped seeking it. Both seemed
reasonable until they began questioning each other.
Around others, Anya could be cheerful, talkative, and curious. She could begin conversations
without thinking and share her excitement without wondering whether she was disturbing
someone. But around her father, even ordinary words required consideration. She worried about
asking the wrong question or receiving a response that would make her regret speaking. When he
asked her something, she often answered briefly. Sometimes she said nothing at all. Lately,
however, her father seemed to want something different. He wanted her to come out of her room,
sit beside him, and tell him what was happening in her life. She could see that he was lonely. He
had never been particularly close to his parents, his wife, or his children. Perhaps he had never
learned how to express affection in the way she needed. Perhaps he was trying now, in the only
way he knew. But understanding his loneliness did not make sitting beside him any easier.
Another part of Anya refused to accept these explanations so easily. He wanted her to speak now,
but had he not taught her to remain quiet? She should make an effort. He was her father, after all.
And had she not made an effort when she was little? He had been tired then. Perhaps he
genuinely had been. But how many times could a child be turned away before she stopped
returning? She was older now, and people could change. Yet did growing older mean that the
disappointments of childhood no longer mattered? Sometimes she wondered whether she had
become unfair to him. Had she grown so accustomed to expecting rejection that she could no
longer recognise his attempts to reach her? Perhaps she was waiting for him to become the father
she had once wanted, while he was waiting for her to become the daughter who would willingly
sit beside him.
Anya did not want to punish him for the past, yet she could not pretend that it had left nothing
behind. One part of her feared becoming a daughter who neglected her father; the other feared
becoming the little girl who kept approaching him only to be turned away. She wanted to speak
to him without rehearsing every sentence, to tell him about her research, her achievements, and
the small things that made her happy. But she also wanted him to understand why these simple
things had become so difficult. Could he understand feelings she had never expressed? And how
could she express them when speaking to him was precisely what frightened her? Sometimes she
wondered whether he noticed the discomfort. Did he remember the moments she remembered, or
had they been too ordinary to remain in his mind? To him, she might simply have become a quiet
daughter who preferred being alone. She wished she could explain that she had not always been
this way with him. Once, she had wanted to tell him everything.
One evening, her father asked Anya to sit beside him. She hesitated at the doorway. Go and sit.
He is trying. But what would she talk about? It did not have to be anything important. Then why
did even an ordinary conversation seem so difficult? She could ask him about his day. What if he
answered in the same impatient tone she remembered from childhood? Perhaps he would not.
Perhaps things were different now. Eventually, she entered the room and sat down. For a while,
neither spoke. He looked at his phone, and Anya looked around the room, trying to remember the
last time she had entered without being asked. She considered telling him about her internship,
but he remained quiet, and she could not find a way to begin. “Did you need anything?” he
eventually asked. She shook her head. “No.” It was such a small answer, yet she felt the familiar
frustration returning. She wanted to explain that her silence was not a rejection, that sometimes
she genuinely did not know how to behave around him. But how could she tell her father that she
was uncomfortable in his presence without hurting him? She remained seated for a little longer
before returning to her room.
Later, Anya wondered whether she should have stayed or tried to speak. Was he attempting to
repair something between them, or did he simply expect her to behave as though nothing had
ever been wrong? Perhaps she had been unfair to him. Perhaps he had been unfair to her. Perhaps
both were true. She did not know whether she wanted an apology, a conversation, or simply the
ability to sit beside him without feeling afraid. She remembered the father who had cared for her
when she was sick, just as she remembered the little girl who had wanted him to listen, to smile
at her achievements, or to agree to a family photograph. Neither memory cancelled the other.
Perhaps the next time he asked her to sit with him, she would go. Perhaps they would find
something to talk about. Or perhaps they would remain in the same uncomfortable silence, each
waiting for the other to make it easier.
For years, Anya had believed that the distance between them would disappear if one of them
finally made an effort. But now that he seemed to be reaching toward her, she had discovered
something she had not expected. She no longer knew how to reach back. What troubled her most
was that she was no longer certain whether she was waiting for him to come closer, or whether
she had forgotten how to let him.

title: The day I die
author: Tinkori
imageAlt: Cover image for The day I die

runs.text: The day I die.
The day that I die,
I will not wake up in the flower fields nor in boiling acid.
I will not go to heaven or hell and the evidence will be in a sarco pod in Sweden or in the reflecting light
of the knife on my kitchen floor.
I will wander these streets I've lived among all my life,
Carefree and alone.
I will learn how to climb a tree and dangle my naked feet from the high branches
oblivious of the view from below.
I will find my favorite shirt amongst the dead fabrics of the world and wrap it around my shoulders again
and no one will be there to sneer “no.”
I will sit in the comfort of the dent I'd made in the cushions of my couch, foot up on the headboard with
the other on the floor,
Relaxed and sated alone in my own home.
They will wail “ Oh, what a waste!” and whisper “so selfish!” when the cameras no longer roll.
And the sun will rise again and the tides will return once more, to shore.
And when they finally let my ashes float in the name of all that is holy
or throw the last spade of dirt over my corpse
When my skin starts to rot.
The day that I die,
My body will finally be my own again,
In a way it hasn't been since I was four.

title: Decomposition
author: Paravin

runs.text: Are bones jealous of flesh?
Rotting away doesn't quite sound like the ideal fate. But for carefully
constructed structures of calcium, that must remain as they are for the rest
of time, it must be riveting.
Flesh sees rotting as just that– rotting. Nothing special, that is their function
after death. Critters will consume whatever is left and leave. But to the
bones, that is movement. That is living.
You're not understanding the beauty of it, are you?
How can decomposition ever be equal to living? They're almost direct
opposites, no? But to the bug, rotting flesh is another day. That bug is
another day for a bird, and so on and so forth. The remaining parts melt
away in the dirt, feeding the land that raised it. Flesh is never truly dead. It'll
continue on with life, be it vicariously. The warmth of the human body may
have left its home, but it'll travel. It'll stay.
Bones however, can only spectate. They can only watch as insects and
microscopic creatures ignore their presence to reach the true nectar– flesh.
Bones may only watch. What choice do they have? No amount of waiting
will free them. Free them from what exactly? Well, the ribcage is a cage,
isn't it? So to them, what difference divides rotting and walking?
Rotting away is seen as the opposite of active life because it's believed to
happen only after death, only in a completely soulless, lightless body buried
under six feet of dirt. Isn't it obvious? The leaves that dry up in winter only
to come back in summer don't agree.
Decomposition doesn't require soil and cold blood, the calendar stuck on
the last day that was truly lived, the alarm clock tired of not ringing, the
eternally unopened windows that feel as if they themselves are afraid of the
sun, and the bed permanently indented by a warm silhouette, know that
fact all too well.
The body resting on the bed is neither dead, nor rotting. Not visibly, at least.
The flesh, though scarce, hasn't begun dissipating. So where exactly is it
decomposing?
Where isn't it decomposing?
What difference is there between a motionless body, incapable of living,
and the bones stuck under it? Spectators, live viewers – that's what they
are. The flesh can barely play its role. Dull, flaky skin scattered with random
bruises and injection marks. But not like the flesh outside. The fleshbags
outside, they truly live, in the complete sense of the word. They run and
they fall, each of their bruises has its own story. Their bones have no
control.
The flesh covering this body is not willingly inadequate, no, not at all. It's
flesh, it wants to do what all flesh does– live. But it's smart enough to know
it doesn't possess the structure to do so. It's not as if the bones have taken
over by choice, they've had to. To protect what's left of the flesh. The
ribcage wants to simply do its job, protect organs. It didn't choose to cage
the entire being. This body lives as a skeleton out of necessity.
Even it knows it can't afford to be as soft as the ones outside.
In this non-dead body, it's the flesh that's jealous, and not of the bags that
somewhat look like it and move around freely– no, it's jealous of the flesh
rotting away. At the very least, rotting flesh has a purpose.
But so does lively flesh, why not be envious of that? Because this flesh can
easily imagine decomposition. The humanely living we speak of? Not even
a possibility to this hopeless mound of meat.
The bones? They have no preference. To them, living and decomposing
aren't opposites. They're both change, and change is an impossible fate for
them.

title: Newspapers
author: Paravin

runs.text: “It's the 21st century, why are you still paying for newspapers every day?”
This is a question I asked my father a long time ago. It seemed downright
silly to me. He has a phone, he reads news on that phone, yet insists on
paying for dailies. My father, being the man he is, simply replied with a
smile and continued flipping through the pages filled with olds rather than
news.
Our TV rack is filled with paper recounting news from before my existence
itself was news, and the library with used up notebooks which themselves
are overflowing with prescriptions, calculations and the drawings of a
younger me. I complained to my father that they take up space and collect
dust. He always shows me my old drawings, a father and daughter holding
hands, drawn with crayons and unadulterated love. I tell him to throw them
away– there's no reason to keep them. His reply is the same as it always
is, a tight-lipped, light-hearted smile, as if he just heard a joke in passing.
I never really understood my father. He always seemed so detached from
me. Or maybe I detached from him. I never really tried to understand either.
Baba existed as a silly acquaintance that happened to contribute to 50% of
my being. My father just, existed.
My father who never cries, not even while recounting stories about his own
father whom he misses so dearly, cried while watching a romance movie.
My mom shook her head quietly, used to her husband's reactions. Of
course, I was crying too, even then I noticed his reddened eyes and quiet
sniffles through the end credits.
That single scene rewired how I saw my father. I realized why he still reads
newspapers and keeps dust collecting stacks of paper.
Because somehow, to my oblivious self, my sentimentality towards old
letters, torn and taped together books, and scratched up pictures of my
loved ones always seemed to be all mine. Clearly not something I inherited
from my extremely stoic mom. It never occurred to me that the tears I shed
whilst reading the book my grandfather left me were my father's first. The
pages I reread to understand better, were racking my father's mind first.
I won't claim to understand him fully, of course I don't know the exact
thought process behind his hoarding. However, if I had been here before
him, I would read the daily paper because my father did. Maybe the words
on the sheets could bring back the smile he'd put on reading something he
already knows. Maybe the paper itself would sting me with the same paper
cuts my father carried on his fingers. And when he’s gone, maybe the
paper could give me back my father.
Maybe that's what the newspapers mean to my father –It's possible they
remind him of my grandfather. The educated, strict, but quirky professor I
never really knew. I don't think my father knew him too well, either. Maybe
his sentimentality is a way to know him, to know us, to remember us.
I always told myself I was the crybaby of the family, the reminiscer.
Completely foreign to my calm and collected mother and brother. But my
singularity was of my own making. My indifference towards my father was
my own choice. Why did I consider the old letters in my box precious, but
the notebooks in the library an outlet for asthma? Because I wasn't ready to
admit that I am the daughter of that silly man.
Now? Maybe I'll get to know him better, draw him some less juvenile
pictures.

I tell him to throw them away– there's no reason to keep them. His reply is the same as it always is, a tight-lipped, light-hearted smile, as if he just heard a joke in passing.

I never really understood my father. He always seemed so detached from me. Or maybe I detached from him. I never really tried to understand either. Baba existed as a silly acquaintance that happened to contribute to 50% of my being. My father just, existed.

My father who never cries, not even while recounting stories about his own father whom he misses so dearly, cried while watching a romance movie. My mom shook her head quietly, used to her husband's reactions. Of course, I was crying too, even then I noticed his reddened eyes and quiet sniffles through the end credits.
That single scene rewired how I saw my father. I realized why he still reads newspapers and keeps dust collecting stacks of paper.

Because somehow, to my oblivious self, my sentimentality towards old letters, torn and taped together books, and scratched up pictures of my loved ones always seemed to be all mine. Clearly not something I inherited from my extremely stoic mom. It never occurred to me that the tears I shed whilst reading the book my grandfather left me were my father's first. The pages I reread to understand better, were racking my father's mind first.

I won't claim to understand him fully, of course I don't know the exact thought process behind his hoarding. However, if I had been here before him, I would read the daily paper because my father did. Maybe the words on the sheets could bring back the smile he'd put on reading something he already knows. Maybe the paper itself would sting me with the same paper cuts my father carried on his fingers. And when he’s gone, maybe the paper could give me back my father.

Maybe that's what the newspapers mean to my father –It's possible they remind him of my grandfather. The educated, strict, but quirky professor I never really knew. I don't think my father knew him too well, either. Maybe his sentimentality is a way to know him, to know us, to remember us.

I always told myself I was the crybaby of the family, the reminiscer. Completely foreign to my calm and collected mother and brother. But my singularity was of my own making. My indifference towards my father was my own choice. Why did I consider the old letters in my box precious, but the notebooks in the library an outlet for asthma? Because I wasn't ready to admit that I am the daughter of that silly man.
Now? Maybe I'll get to know him better, draw him some less juvenile pictures.

runs.text: Somewhere, a young girl is reading romance books under the warmth of
her blanket, flashlight in hand, and squealing over these scenes. She'll
clutch the book to her chest so that her thumping heart may read it too. Ah!
There it is! The word–
Love.
Romance, confessions under downpour, candlelit dinners, bouquets of
roses, and wedding bells. This is the fantasia. When the stars align, she'll
meet the one. The soulmate, the destiny. That's love.
As she grows up, the lack of the passion ingrained in those pages she read
so many years ago will show itself to her. Confessions enshrouded in rain
water are accompanied by the annoyance of having to buy another
umbrella, candlelit dinners are battles of splitting the bill, roses wilt away
faster than you can say “how much are these?” and wedding bells are the
markers of multi-thousand dollar weddings.
She wonders why love doesn't reach her. Why the love targeted towards
her is so capitalistic. Maybe she had torn out cupid's luscious golden curls
in her last life, and he wants revenge for his lost strands. Or maybe it's just
her destiny to never feel love. Love exists only in the storybooks and
movies.
And when she sobs about her lackluster love life, her best friend will hand
over her favorite ice cream flavor and assure her it's not the end. When it
rains, her mother will make her mushroom soup because she knows her
daughter loves having it in rainy weather. When the power goes out, her
siblings will light candles so they can continue playing UNO with her. When
she complains about how loud and annoying the wedding bells at the
nearby church are, her cat will only gaze up at her and tilt his head,
meow
She'll stay wrapped in the belief that love just doesn't exist in her world.
Because we– yes you, dear reader, and the author– have more blind spots
than we think. We can't see love unless it's in red wrapping paper, tied with
a pink silk bow with the price tag attached.
But love is everywhere. Love is in the little girl’s eyes when she sees the
pitter patter of rain outside her window, and it's in the bystanders’ smiles
watching her play in it, her joy infectious. Love is in the rough hands of the
florist who made the bouquet of roses, and in the busy civilians who stop to
take a look at the beautiful arrangements in the neighborhood flower shop.
It's in the onlookers watching a couple beaming to get married after their
union finally became legal.
And for our protagonist? Of course it's in her best friend and her family, but
it's also in her. It's in her kindness, her smile, her presence. It's in her
classmates wondering why she's been absent. It's in her explaining the rain
made her catch a fever and everyone's encouragement to feel better soon.
Love to humans is like fish to water– the author isn't very sure either of
them can see it surrounding themselves and everything in their vicinities.
Fish don't realize they're out of water until they can't breathe, and we don't
realize how much love truly exists in our life.
But maybe that's our give and take. We're blessed to be surrounded by
love everywhere, but our human senses cannot sniff it out, the rose
coloured glasses make it harder to see anything at all. Fortunately, glasses
are famously removable.
And our protagonist can continue reading her romance books, maybe
under a different light. After all, reading with a flashlight is kind of difficult.

“But we can’t. It’s forbidden...”
“Is it okay? Only for today?”
A surprise she had never expected.
Surely not from him.
“But it’s risky”
“I know, but shall we?
Just for today...”
“So we go back to usual tomorrow?
We forget what happened?
Tomorrow, we’ll be all ‘professional’
and all ‘commercial’?”
She asked as the sound
of her breaths blurred that of rain.
As her heart ran towards him
and she felt an entire forest in her stomach,
breaking the rules she had constructed
and imposed for months.
“Not here, not him,
those eyes
those very eyes
would be your doom.”
she told herself.
But in the end she sank,
“However you want it to be”
her heart heard his words,
her rules sat in the corner
like a child in ‘time-out’.
A screen and the internet
kept their bodies
in two separate places,
but their souls...
And the tension!
It let the wall of confidence
she built whimper;
and made the
lifeless reactions he mastered
gasp for air.
Abontee Ahmed
Then ‘tomorrow’ came.
They had to ‘forget it’
they had to be ‘normal’
but her heart
was anything but normal.
So she lost herself again,
she
caught him by surprise this time.
He leaned on the concrete
while she leaned on him;
gasping for air,
while their fingers
traced each other.
But she wasn’t allowed
to lose herself,
to drown in those eyes,
to make him warm;
even if she wanted to.
For she
was made of flames
and he,
dry wood.
So he left,
vanished from her life
with no trace.
There should’ve been words,
but there weren’t.
None.
So she sat by her window
with her flute in her hand
and thought,
only if she could
rewind time...
Even if she could,
would she ask him
what her heart
actually wanted to?
Abontee Ahmed
Would she ask:
“What if I don’t want to forget?
What if I want
this
to last?
What if I want you,
again and again,
and forever?
What if I wanna wrap myself
in
your
arms as I cup your face
and place my forehead on yours?
What if I want those
slightly asymmetrical eyes
to trace my skin?
What if I say I want to
wake up to that smile
showcasing your
crooked teeth?
What if I want you to taste
the lemon-mint tea I just had?
What if I want you
to draw
me
like
Jack drew his Rose?
What if I want to hear
I’m chuffed’
way, way more often?
What if I want us
to sip steaming hot
a little too sweet tea,
while it rains outside?
What if I want ‘
Us
’ to be,
to
exist?
But she knows she wouldn’t.
She wasn’t allowed
to ask him those,
nor to spread her arms,
and become his;
even if she wanted to.
For she…
And he…

As if they were trembling, holding back their tears. Far above, the mountain of Croatia kept its grief silent. The snow settled over him, gathering like a heavy covering, hiding what the world had done to him. Far away, Elm street has stayed dark and indifferent about the cold night. And the snow went on falling gently over a stillness that no kindness could ever undo.The letter may be found, if at all, only as a smear of ink in the mud.
A person exists twice, once in the world and once in the minds of those who love him.And if the only one who remembered him was the snow, did he exist once, or twice?
